text:
Put a microphone in front of its
own speaker and turn the gain up.

Below a certain point you
get an echo that dies away.
Past that point you get a howl,

and the howl settles on
whatever note the room likes.
Nobody chose the note. The room did.

That point has a name.
Loop gain equal to one.

This is a video about a week we spent
finding that point in two places it was

not supposed to be,
and about how we found it,
because the how is the part you can use.

It started as art. Two concept
briefs for interactive pieces,

written by Lex, the reviewer on this
project, in two different vocabularies.

The first is about a feed. Everything
that reaches you arrives framed:

a card, a timestamp, a sentiment
colour, a "because you liked".

The brief's claim is one sentence:
every frame applied re-enters as signal.

Whatever you do to the feed
becomes one more thing in the feed.

The second is about pollution,
read as a symptom.

Push a signal out of awareness and it
accumulates somewhere, and comes back.
The brief's claim is also one sentence:

excluding the signal repeats
the act that produced it.

An art programme called Phase Transition
asked us to translate a finding into

a form, under the rule carry the
structure, not just the essence.

The programme's name gave us a
question to put to both briefs.

As you turn the system up,
does it slide, or does it drop?

You cannot ask a brief that
question. You can ask a model.

So the first thing we
did, for each brief,

was write its rules down
plainly enough to run.

The feed became a stream
from seven channels,

four that ask something of the reader
and three she would rather see, ranked

by stated weights. Every gesture returns
to the stream two point two seconds

later as one more item. Four
numbers wear down by stated rules:

attention, calm, agency, and the
minutes she meant for something else.

Then seeds. A seed is a number
that fixes every random choice,

so the same seed gives the
same session on any machine.

When a run looks strange,
you run that one again.

We say "twenty seeds a point" and we
mean twenty repeatable sessions at each
setting.

None of this is a claim about a person.
It is a machine for finding out what

the rules entail. That
sentence will come back.
The second brief had been written,

read and extended by two people before
anyone wrote down the number that decides

it. Here it is. Each exclusion
deposits a unit in the exterior.
A unit returns with some probability,

and a returned signal is excluded
again with some propensity,

and comes back louder by a gain.
So one exclusion begets,

on average, propensity times
gain times return share,
exclusions in the next generation.
Epidemiologists call that R‑nought.

Below one, it dies out.
Above one, it multiplies.

The brief's claim that ignoring the
signal supplies fresh material for the

next return is the claim
that the gain is above one.

Before we ran anything we
wrote five hypotheses to disk,

with numbers, and what
would falsify each.

With our constants the critical
propensity was zero point eight.

We marked the section and
did not touch it again.

This costs ten minutes. It is the
difference between a result and a story.

We swept the feed first.
Four constants through a range,

twenty-four points, ten
or twenty seeds a point.

Interval between arrivals from twelve
seconds down to a third of a second.

No cliff. Every curve
flat or sliding. One knee,

near three and a half
seconds between arrivals,

which happens to be
the page's normal day.

And the knee had a reason we
could read off the rules by hand.

Attention in the model recovers
only after three seconds of quiet.

The share of gaps that long is a
continuous function of the interval,
one above five seconds, zero below two.

The attention curves track it at
point nine to point nine nine seven.
A slope, with an explanation.

Then the exclusion loop. We had predicted
a critical point at zero point eight

and said the sweep would
read it as a cliff.

It read "slides." Our first
hypothesis failed under its own test.

Here is why, and it
is worth sitting with.

The verdict rule was written for the feed,
for a bounded quantity that steps.

A quantity that diverges at a
critical point does not step.

It grows, and in a three-minute
session it grows smoothly straight

through the critical value. The
instrument was wrong for the question.

The pre-registration is
what let us see that,
instead of quietly moving the goalposts.

So we wrote a second test
and labelled it post-hoc,

so nobody could mistake
it for the first.

For a critical point the right question
is whether the end state depends on

how long the session
ran. Below the point,

a twelve-minute session should
end where a three-minute one did.
Above it, it should keep growing.

At zero point six the
ratio was one point one.
At zero point eight, three point nine.

At zero point nine, sixty-two. The
turn was at zero point eight, where

the number said. And the
failure stays in the record,
at full length, next to the success.

Some claims do not need a sample.
They follow from the rules alone.

For those we used Lean,
a proof assistant,
in its core form with no library,

so that anyone can check
them with one small download.

The band cannot be kept flat by
acting. The floor never comes down.

The moment's calm deficit
persists as structure.

Agency never rises without a
like that worked or an emptying.

For the loop: supercritical
mass is unbounded,
subcritical mass is bounded,

and a higher return rate
never lowers R‑nought.

Twenty-one theorems, resting on
Lean's own axioms and nothing else.

One of them corrected us. Our first
version of the floor theorem was false

as written. If the floor
were ever above its cap,

a rule would pull it back down. The
compiler found the missing hypothesis.
That is what a proof assistant is for.

And every theorem is of the form: if the
model is as written, then this follows.

Not one is about a person.
The proofs tell you,

by what they cannot reach,
where the simulator's work begins.

Lex's extension of the second
brief had put a body in the model:

each exclusion costs something,
an allostatic load that recovers slowly.

We had three readings
of what the load does.
Then we read Wegner.

Wegner's ironic process theory says why
trying not to think of something makes

you think of it. A monitor scans
for the suppressed thought and,

in scanning, keeps it close. Under load
the monitor keeps running while the

effort to suppress gets tired.
In the model's terms,
load raises the return rate.

We wrote the prediction first. The
critical point would barely move, because

the return share was already point
eight three and doubling the rate could

only buy the rest. That held. We also
wrote that the frame would be small.
That was wrong by an order of magnitude.

R‑nought counts returns per generation
and says nothing about how long

a generation takes. Double the return
rate and you barely move whether the

loop runs away. You halve
the time a generation takes,

so above the threshold it
compounds twice as fast.

R‑nought says whether. The
return rate says how fast.
We did not have that sentence on Monday.

Which is when the two briefs
stopped being neighbours.

In the feed, a gesture returns once,
as itself, and the echo does not act.

R‑nought is zero. The share
accumulates and ages out.
A slope.

In the exclusion loop, a return invites
the act that produced it and comes

back louder. R‑nought is positive, and a
positive R‑nought has a critical point.
A cliff.

Every frame re-enters as signal.
Excluding the signal repeats the act.

The same loop, at gain
zero and gain above zero.

The difference between media
theory and depth psychology,

in these two models, is one rule:
does what returns invite an act?

So that is what we made. Three minutes.
One stream of pings, read three ways.

The line: a real run of the
feed's model, with its sounds.

A gesture, and its
pop two seconds later.
Loop gain zero.

The loop: the same pings through a
delay with gain, rising past one.

The echoes stop dying. The howl.
A resonance placed by hand at

eight hundred and seventy hertz, as a
room has one, and we say so on screen.

The plate: the howl's settled
note drives a plate of sand,

and the sand leaves where the plate
moves and gathers where it is still.

Chladni, seventeen eighty-seven.
A continuous drive,

a threshold, a form. The oldest
version of the same structure.

Two people did this. A public
repository, a laptop, a week.

One of us built with an AI
assistant; the other reviewed,
on purpose with a different one,

so we would not share
one set of blind spots.

She asked to be credited as a reviewer
rather than an author, because
that is what she did.

Here is what we would say to anyone
who wants to do their own research and

means it. Write the rules
down. Seed everything.

Predict first, with a number.
Keep the failures at full length.

Prove what can be proved
and say what cannot.

Find the quantity the question turns on.
Work with someone who reads against
you.

And say what the numbers are not. Every
claim in this video is about a model.
Whether a feed does any of this to you,

whether your own loop has a gain, is a
question for a person and a measurement.

That experiment is the
one nobody has run.
It is next.
